title: The face grows bright
hook: in the company of the holy the face grows bright and filth is washed

segments.voice: Yesterday, acharaj: God beyond reach, and the wondrous story of the holy. Your line was good company. Today, the first stanza of ashtpadi seven.

There's an old saying: tell me who your friends are, and I'll tell you who you are. Parents say a version of it to teenagers; coaches say it to athletes. Underneath it is something plain: we soak up the people we sit with, their words, their moods, their habits, the jokes we start telling the way they tell them. Guru Arjan says it too, and he says it as good news. The first stanza of ashtpadi seven begins with a face that changes.
screen: `TELL ME WHO YOUR FRIENDS ARE.` → `WE SOAK UP WHO WE SIT WITH.` → `A FACE THAT CHANGES.`

segments.voice: Saadh, you met yesterday: a holy person. Sangat is company, the people you're with. Together, saadh sangat: the company of the holy. For Sikhs, sangat on its own also names the congregation, the people sitting together before the Guru Granth Sahib. The stanza opens: saadh kai sang mukh oojal hot. In the company of the holy, the face becomes bright. Oojal is bright, clean, radiant. In Punjabi, a bright face is also a way of talking about honor, the opposite of a face blackened with shame. So you look lighter, and you can hold your head up. Then: saadhsang mal sagalee khot. In the holy company, all the filth is washed off. Mal is grime, the kind that builds up without your noticing. Neither line says the holy company scrubs you. It's quieter than that. You sit with good people and some of their brightness rubs off on your face. You spend time where the Name is sung, and the grime you didn't know you were carrying starts to loosen. The stanza doesn't make it a matter of rules or effort. It describes it the way you'd describe sunlight: sit in it and you warm up. That's why, for Sikhs, going to the sangat matters, not just reading alone. The company is part of the medicine.
screen: `SAADH: HOLY. SANGAT: COMPANY.` · `OOJAL: THE FACE GROWS BRIGHT.` · `MAL: THE GRIME WASHES OFF.` · `LIKE SITTING IN SUNLIGHT.` · then, large: `COMPANY SHAPES YOU.`

segments.voice: Picture someone good you could spend time with, a call, a walk, a meal, and imagine you're already beside them. Let your face relax, the forehead, the eyes, the mouth, the way a face does in good company; it already knows how. If you pray, you can ask to be good company for someone else, too.
Saadh sangat. The company of the holy, where, the stanza says, the face grows bright and the grime washes off.
Your line: company shapes you. Good company works the way sunlight does, with no scrubbing at all. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 463 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: EGO LEAVES IN GOOD COMPANY.`

what a scholar hears: 'mukh oojal' is idiomatic for honor (as 'kaalaa mukh' is for disgrace); 'sangat' is also the everyday Sikh word for the congregation.

chat.says: Why go to the gurdwara so often? Can't I just read and pray at home?
options: You can, but the stanza says company itself changes you: the face grows bright, grime washes off.
No, prayer at home doesn't count; only prayer said inside the gurdwara is ever heard.
The stanza says the sangat scrubs you clean by its rules, whether you like it or not.
